clue.text: Ultimately penned by innocent child, a letter on papyrus, perhaps?

parts.note: a lamb is the byword for an innocent young thing, and 'child' asks for the young one rather than the grown sheep

indicators.note: 'Ultimately' means at the very end, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is taken.

parts.note: the closing letter of 'penned'
used literally, lifted straight out of the surface

explanation.surface: A letter written on papyrus, apparently by an innocent child, and signed off at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Papyrus points at the ancient world, so 'letter' is a character from an alphabet and not something posted — the sheet the surface hands you is the wrong sort of writing altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: LAMBDA is the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, and 'on papyrus' flags a character written in antiquity rather than a note in the post.

clue.text: Critical evaluation, turning of tides indeed?

indicators.note: in, the front part of the clue word indeed, puts the scrambled letters within the deed

parts.note: a deed is an act, something done

indicators.note: turning of means the letters of tides are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the turn of the tide is a real test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'indeed' must be split into 'in' and 'deed', which the question mark hints at; inside goes IDTES, the letters of 'tides' rearranged by 'turning of'.
explanation.definitionFit: A decisive trial that shows whether something is genuine or works is called by this name.

clue.text: Someone loathing vampire, point driven through heart — might this cover the body?

indicators.note: A stake driven through the heart goes into the middle, so the letter it carries lands at the centre of the other piece.

parts.note: a vampire takes bat form, so someone loathing one is a bat hater — two words running together into eight letters
west is a point of the compass, and its initial is the usual shorthand

explanation.surface: Someone who hates vampires driving a stake clean through the creature's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' reads as the sharpened end of the stake and is a compass direction. The question mark is the setter admitting his definition describes what the stuff does rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Run a bath and the water covers whoever gets in, so the definition works by describing the effect instead of offering a synonym.

clue.text: Duck under perfect child in martial art

indicators.note: In a down entry 'under' is literal geography: the piece it governs is written at the foot of the column, below everything else.

parts.note: A1 means top quality, and the 1 is written as a capital I once it joins a word
a kid is a child
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, and nothing is written as O

explanation.surface: Somebody ducking underneath a faultless youngster at a martial arts class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the move the class would teach you and is the cricket score of nothing, one of the handful of sporting words a British setter treats as common property.
explanation.definitionFit: Aikido is one of the Japanese martial arts, so the definition names the category and leaves the letters to pick which member is meant.

clue.text: A parting bicycle travelling, getting away from relations

indicators.note: A parting separates things, and this one splits the shuffled letters so the single letter can drop into the gap.
Letters that are travelling do not stay at the address they were given, so they arrive in a different order.

parts.note: one letter taken literally from the farewell in the picture
seven letters of raw material, handed over whole

explanation.surface: A goodbye at the roadside as somebody pedals off into the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A parting' reads as the farewell, which is exactly why the A slips past unnoticed as a letter. 'Relations' means family on the surface and something quite different underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Celibacy is abstention from sexual relations, so 'relations' takes its other sense and the phrase names the state as a noun would.

clue.text: On which it's cold and bitter after temperature in liquid decreasing?

definitions.text: On which it's cold and bitter after temperature in liquid decreasing?

indicators.note: after places the cold and bitter pieces behind everything else
in says the temperature letter goes inside the jumbled word
liquid suggests something fluid, so the letters of decreasing flow into a new order

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
bitter is a type of ale, the classic British pub beer

explanation.surface: A wry look at a thermometer: cold, bitter weather as the temperature drops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid' rearranges DECREASING to CENIGRADES, and 'in' puts T inside it to give CENTIGRADES; 'after' sets C and ALE behind that. The whole clue describes a thermometer reading falling.
explanation.definitionFit: The Celsius temperature measure starts with freezing at zero, so falling readings on it mean bitter cold.

clue.text: Feeling ready for tennis achievement

parts.note: the feeling, taken as the plain noun
somebody game for anything is ready for it

explanation.surface: Being in the mood for a knock-up on the tennis court.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis 'love' is nothing at all, the score you have to hold an opponent to for six straight points, so the warm feeling of the surface is the wrong sense twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: A love game is one won without the loser taking a single point, love being tennis's word for zero, which makes it a genuine achievement.

clue.text: Drill, tedious thing?

definitions.meaning: the tool that turns and cuts its way into a wall
anything that sends you to sleep, the agent noun made from the verb

explanation.surface: Somebody dismissing a drill — the repetitive kind — as a thoroughly dull way to spend a morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves come off the same verb: to bore a hole and to bore a person. The question mark covers 'thing', since the word more often names a beetle or a bit than an occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: A borer is the tool that drills a hole, and anything that bores you is a borer as well — one sense mechanical, one social.

clue.text: Preserving wood, one going in strong, ecofreak?

indicators.note: 'Going in' sends the single letter into the middle of the others rather than leaving it at either end.
The FREAK at the back of this word is the instruction — a freak is something formed wrongly, so the letters come out misshapen.

parts.note: the numeral one written as a letter, the oldest trick in the book
six letters of raw material, used exactly as spelt
only the front half of this word is material, three more letters for the mixture; the back half is the instruction

explanation.surface: An eco-warrior wading in hard against somebody treating their timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ecofreak' is one word in the clue and two in the wordplay: the ECO is material and the FREAK is the instruction. Splitting a word down the middle like that is a Paul regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Creosote is the tarry liquid painted onto fences and sleepers to stop them rotting, so creosoting is precisely the act of preserving wood.

clue.text: Ill-conceived, a plastic boyfriend on film

indicators.note: In an across row a piece sitting 'on' another is written after it, the way words lean rightwards along the line.

parts.note: a film is a thin layer, and a thin layer of water in the air is mist
used literally
Barbie's boyfriend is a doll, so 'plastic' names what he is made of rather than insulting him

explanation.surface: A film with a hopelessly artificial boyfriend in it, and a badly judged one at that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' does two jobs on the surface, insincere and literally moulded, and only the literal one leads anywhere. Ken has been Barbie's boyfriend since 1961.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mistaken is wrongly judged or wrongly conceived, so 'ill-conceived' is the same idea in adjective form and swaps in without a wobble.

clue.text: Partner once put on green top

indicators.note: Put one piece on another along an across row and it goes after it, pushed along to the right.

parts.note: vert is the heraldic name for green, the colour as a herald would blazon it
a former partner is an ex

explanation.surface: An old flame turning up dressed in green.
explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry supplies 'vert' for green, one of a small set of blazon words — gules for red, sable for black — that setters reach for whenever a colour is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A vertex is the highest point of a figure or a hill, so 'top' is the everyday noun for the same place.

clue.text: Train carriage required with this?

definitions.meaning: on the surface these are two railway words in a row, one of them the thing the other is made of
read the other way, the sentence is asking what needs a train, and 'carriage' becomes the bearing of the person carrying one

explanation.surface: A railway question: which sort of carriage does a train need?
explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here — the whole sentence is the definition, with 'train' switching from rails to the length of fabric that trails behind a bride down the aisle.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding dress is the garment that comes with a train, the trailing fabric a bride carries behind her, so the question describes it exactly.

clue.text: Monsters had been identified as footballers

parts.note: 'had been' is the plural past of 'to be'
Wolverhampton Wanderers are Wolves to every English football fan, and a club's nickname stands in for its players

explanation.surface: Monsters turning out, on investigation, to be a football team.
explanation.walkthrough: English club nicknames are standard crossword currency — Wolves for Wolverhampton Wanderers, Spurs for Tottenham — and here the plural does the joining work for free.
explanation.definitionFit: Werewolves are the men who turn into wolves at full moon, monsters in the plainest storybook sense of the word.

clue.text: See 2 Down
Megastar at sea port

indicators.note: Being at sea is being lost with no bearings, and letters with no bearings do not stay in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: eight letters of raw material — the celebrity is there for the picture only

explanation.surface: A celebrity adrift somewhere off the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Ramsgate is a Channel port in Kent, on the corner of England nearest the continent, and the kind of British place name a daily puzzle assumes you have ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramsgate is a working harbour town on the Kent coast, so 'port' defines it by category and the anagram picks out which port is meant.

clue.text: Cat still gripping tail of dog, another cat upset about that

indicators.note: about means going around, so the overturned cat wraps the rest
upset in a down clue turns the word upside down, so it reads backwards

parts.note: a mog or moggy is British slang for a cat

indicators.note: gripping means holding inside, so the word for still takes in the dog's last letter

parts.note: still means motionless, inert

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter, here of dog

explanation.surface: One cat holds a dog's tail in its teeth while another cat, upset, looks on.
explanation.walkthrough: INERT (still) grips G, the tail of dog, making INGERT; MOG, another cat, is upset to GOM and goes about that.
explanation.definitionFit: A male cat with orange fur is commonly called this in Britain.

clue.text: Bugs Bunny's first song about carrot extremely emotional at first

indicators.note: Bunny's first is the opening letter of Bunny

parts.note: only its first letter is used

indicators.note: about means around, so the song is wrapped round the following letters

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in opera

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so the two end letters of carrot

parts.note: only its outside letters are used

indicators.note: at first picks the opening letter of emotional

parts.note: only its first letter is used

explanation.surface: Bugs Bunny bursts into a heartfelt song about his favourite carrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs Bunny' reads as the cartoon rabbit, but Bugs alone is the definition. ARIA goes about CT (carrot's ends) and E, after the B.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugs is an informal word for germs or microbes, which are bacteria.

clue.text: Bounty boarded by a mutineer finally, astern

indicators.note: a ship boarded by people has them inside it, so the next letters go inside

parts.note: a bounty is a reward offered

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of mutineer

parts.note: only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: The mutiny on HMS Bounty, with a rebel finally climbing aboard at the stern.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bounty is the famous mutiny ship, but here it is just a reward; A and R go inside REWARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern means towards the back of a ship, so heading backwards or to the rear.

clue.text: Baseball team certainly not heard of in Europe?

indicators.note: 'Heard' asks for a sound rather than a spelling, and 'in Europe' says which language to say it in — the German for no.

parts.note: the German for a flat refusal is nein, and said aloud that is an English number

explanation.surface: Baseball sides being something nobody in Europe has ever heard of.
explanation.walkthrough: German nein is a plain no, and 'certainly not' is that no with feeling — the small stretch the question mark is there to apologise for.
explanation.definitionFit: A baseball team fields nine players, so the number is its standing nickname, the way a cricket team is an eleven.

clue.text: Caught in German town, you've been captured!

indicators.note: 'In' is the plainest container instruction there is: what comes before it goes inside what comes after.

parts.note: Gotha is a town in Thuringia, in the middle of Germany
c for caught is how a cricket scorecard records a catch

explanation.surface: Somebody being seized in the middle of a German town.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket's scorecard supplies the c for caught, and it goes into a town most solvers only ever meet in crosswords. The exclamation mark is the definition's tone of voice, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Gotcha is what you shout the moment you have got someone, so the definition quotes the captor's line instead of offering a synonym.

clue.text: Villa's place secured in prize museum piece

indicators.note: Something secured in a place is fastened inside it, so those letters are locked within the word that follows.

parts.note: a rosette is the ribbon badge pinned on a winner at a show
Aston Villa are a Birmingham football club, named after Aston, the district of the city they come from

explanation.surface: A villa's site being fastened into some prize-winning exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: Villa is the football club, so 'place' is the Birmingham district it takes its name from rather than a house in Tuscany, which is where the surface would rather you looked.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rosetta Stone is the inscribed slab that unlocked hieroglyphs, and 'museum piece' names it by where it has sat since 1802, the British Museum.

clue.text: Key tenant initially lost?

indicators.note: What is lost initially is the letter at the start, so the word turns up one letter shorter at the front.

parts.note: somebody who rents a place from a landlord is its tenant

explanation.surface: An important tenant who went missing early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' is the one on a keyboard rather than the one in a lock, and it is the definition, sitting exactly where a solver expects an adjective describing the tenant.
explanation.definitionFit: Enter is the big key you hit to send whatever you have typed, so 'Key' names it by the thing the word is printed on.

clue.text: Embroidered anecdote?

parts.note: read as the surface intends, this is a story someone has stretched considerably in the telling; read the other way it is meant literally, and points at the material embroidery is actually worked in

explanation.surface: A tale somebody has quietly dressed up in the telling.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses sit on top of each other: the exaggerated story, and the thread you would embroider with. Both are the same four letters, which is why the clue needs only three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarn is a long story, and an embroidered one is a story stretched in the telling — while yarn is also the thread embroidery is worked in.

clue.text: Vishnu, leader lost in war following attacks, reportedly?

indicators.note: following places the war letters after the sound of attacks
reportedly means as spoken, here with a dropped H as in casual speech

parts.note: to have at someone is to attack them; said with a dropped H it is 'avat'

indicators.note: the leader of war, its first letter, is lost

parts.note: only its letters after the first are used

explanation.surface: A Hindu god's champion fights on in war after its commander falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have at' is an old cry meaning attack; dropping the H, as some speakers do, gives AVAT. The question mark flags that the answer is a form of Vishnu, not the god himself.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu belief an avatar is an earthly incarnation of a deity, and Vishnu is the god best known for them.

clue.text: Prison, where racketeer has time inside

indicators.note: Doing time inside is doing it in jail, and here the word is meant literally as well: that letter goes within the other piece.

parts.note: a racketeer here is somebody who wields a racket: Carlos Alcaraz, the Spanish tennis champion
the standard one-letter shorthand for time

explanation.surface: The prison where a gangster is currently serving his sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racketeer' is the joke, and it is not the gangster the surface promises but a man holding a tennis racket, whose surname is a single letter away from the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcatraz is the island jail in San Francisco Bay, so 'Prison' defines by category and the most famous instance stands in for the class.

clue.text: Sequence logged by gentleman, resubmitted when typed the wrong way?

indicators.note: To log something is to write it down inside a record, so these are the words the letters are recorded in rather than a description of them.
Typed the wrong way round, a run of letters comes out back to front, which is how it is sitting in the clue.

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the join between these two words, travelling the other way

explanation.surface: A gentleman logging in, getting his details wrong and having to type them all over again.
explanation.walkthrough: The computing picture is doing all the disguising: 'logged', 'typed' and 'sequence' belong to the same world as the answer, so none of them looks like the instruction it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A username is the fixed string of characters you register and type in each time, so 'sequence' names it by its form rather than its job.

clue.text: A loch, out of which pulled the first old nut

indicators.note: Pulling a letter out of a word is a deletion: it leaves, and the letters on either side close up behind it.
There are two of that letter to choose from, and 'the first' settles which one goes — the earlier of the pair.

parts.note: the A of the surface, then Lomond — Loch Lomond is the great loch north of Glasgow, and the name comes over whole
o is the standard shorthand for old, and it names the letter being pulled out

explanation.surface: An old nut fished out of a Scottish loch.
explanation.walkthrough: Loch Lomond is the loch everybody reaches for first and the right one for once, so the work is in spotting that 'old' is a letter rather than part of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: An almond is the nut in marzipan and macaroons, so 'nut' is the plain category word and the wordplay settles which kind.
